History British rule and independence On 25 May 1887 Mombasa was relinquished to the British East Africa Association, later the Imperial British East Africa Company, and came under British administration in 1895. It soon became the capital of the East Africa Protectorate and the sea terminal of the Uganda Railway, construction of which began in 1896. Many workers were brought in from British India to build the railway, and the city's fortunes revived. The Sultan of Zanzibar formally presented the town to the British in 1898. In 1907 the protectorate's capital was moved to Nairobi. Medical officers had warned that Mombasa's swampy ground threatened health, and the Commissioner of the East Africa Protectorate, Sir James Hayes Sadler, urged London to relocate. Nairobi has been Kenya's capital ever since. The Mombasa tusks, one of the city's best-known monuments, were constructed in 1952 by the British administration of the Kenya Colony, commemorating the visit of Queen Elizabeth II.

Suburbs North Coast Nyali, a prime upmarket residential area on the mainland north of the island, is linked by the Nyali Bridge. It has numerous beachfront hotels in the area known as the "North Coast", and two distinct sections — the established Old Nyali and the newer New Nyali. For many residents, Nyali has become self-contained, with shopping malls, cinemas, banks, schools and post offices, reducing the need to cross the bridge into the congested city centre. Nyali is home to the Mamba Village crocodile farm, the Nyali Golf Club and several of the coast's most prestigious schools. Kongowea is a densely populated area with 15 villages and an estimated 106,180 residents at the 2009 census. It is a cosmopolitan settlement mainly inhabited by people who migrated from the mainland in search of work in the service and manufacturing sectors, many employed as watchmen, gardeners, masons and domestic workers in neighbouring Nyali. Its best-known villages — Kisumu Ndogo, Shauri Yako and Mnazi Mmoja — face poor sanitation, high crime and limited access to basic amenities. Kongowea is also home to one of the largest open-air markets in the African Great Lakes region.

Education The major university in the island is the Technical University of Mombasa. The city has a campus of Kenyatta University. Other major university campuses include University of Nairobi-Mombasa campus, Mount Kenya University-Mombasa campus, JKUAT-Mombasa, Shanzu Teachers Training College, Mombasa Technical College, Bandari college, Utalii college, and ICS college Mombasa. International schools which provide International curricula, normally practice the IGCSE system (English curriculum), The Islamic curriculum and the IB curriculum (International Baccalaureate) such as Aga Khan Academy - IB Mombasa Academy - IGCSE Coast Academy - IGCSE Oshwal Academy - IGCSE Light Academy - IGCSE Braeburn Mombasa International School - IGCSE.

Notable people During its history, Mombasa was visited by numerous pioneers of the maritime exploration, such as the Arabs Al Idrissi (1151) and Ibn Battuta (1330) or the Portuguese Vasco da Gama (1498), Pedro Álvares Cabral (1500) João da Nova (1505) and Afonso de Albuquerque (1507). Abdilatif Abdalla, writer, university professor and political protestor Karen Blixen, Danish novelist Mercedes Iman Diamond, drag queen and contestant on the eleventh season of RuPaul's Drag Race Timothy R. McClanahan, marine ecologist who lived and has worked in Mombasa since 1991 Swaleh Nguru, Arab businessman, conservationist and philanthropist Thomas Risley Odhiambo, entomologist Ayub Ogada, musician, singer and composer known for having composed two songs for the movie The Constant Gardener Rodgers Okumu, footballer

Demography Mombasa city had a population of 1,208,333 at the 2019 census. Mombasa has a cosmopolitan population, with the Swahili people and Mijikenda predominant. Other sizeable communities include the Kamba and Taita Bantus as well as Luo, Luhya, Kisii and Kikuyu, many of them drawn from western and central Kenya. Over the centuries, many immigrants and traders have settled in Mombasa, particularly from the Middle East and South Asia. The major religions are Christianity and Islam, with Swahili serving as the lingua franca and English used in government and education.

Geography Being a coastal city, Mombasa is characterised by flat topography. It is centred on Mombasa Island but extends to the mainland. The island is separated from the mainland by two creeks: Tudor Creek to the north and Port Reitz and Kilindini Harbour to the south.

Suburbs South Coast Likoni: a lower-income and lower-middle-class neighbourhood connected to Mombasa Island by ferry. It is south of Mombasa Island and is made up mostly of Swahili and non-Swahili Bantu communities. The ferry channel was the site of the Likoni Riots of 1997. The Liwatoni Pedestrian Floating Bridge, opened in late 2020, was built to ease pressure on the Likoni ferry crossing by carrying most foot traffic, leaving the ferries to serve vehicular and cargo crossing between Mombasa Island and the South Coast. Diani Beach: a beach resort area in Kwale County, some 36 km (22 miles) south of Mombasa on the mainland coast, and a prime resort for local and international tourists. Diani has an airstrip at nearby Ukunda serving direct flights from Nairobi Wilson and other airfields. Mombasa Mainland Magongo: an outlying township about 20 minutes' drive northwest of Mombasa Island, situated on the Nairobi highway. This fringe community has historically lacked effective electricity, water and sewer systems.

Suburbs Mombasa is located on Mombasa Island and sprawls onto the surrounding mainland. The island is connected to the mainland to the north by the Nyali Bridge, to the south by the Likoni Ferry, and to the west by the Makupa Causeway, alongside which runs the Kenya–Uganda Railway. The port serves Kenya and the countries of the interior, linking them to the ocean. The city is served by Moi International Airport, in the northwestern mainland suburb of Chaani. Mombasa Island Kizingo: considered the prime residential area of Mombasa. The State House, the provincial headquarters, the Mombasa Law Courts and the Municipal Council are located in Kizingo, as are the Aga Khan Academy, Aga Khan High School, Serani Primary and High Schools, Coast Academy, Jaffery Academy, Loreto Convent, Mama Ngina Girls' High School and the Government Training Institute (GTI).

Climate Mombasa has a tropical wet-and-dry (savanna) climate, classified Köppen Aw (bordering As on modern Köppen–Geiger maps) and Trewartha Asha. Rainfall is strongly seasonal: the wettest months are April and May, while January and February are the driest. Located near the equator, Mombasa has only slight seasonal temperature variation, with daytime highs ranging 28.4–33.3 °C (83.1–91.9 °F). As a seaport, Mombasa is exposed to the effects of a fluctuating climate. In October 2006 a flood affected 60,000 people. As in the rest of Kenya, climate change is already posing challenges: coastal erosion has become a problem for infrastructure, with the coastline eroding at 2.5–20 cm (0.98–7.87 in) per year because of rising sea levels, increasing annual flooding. During the unusually intense long rains of April–May 2024, floods again displaced thousands of residents across the county.

Economy Mombasa is an important economic centre in Kenya. With a 2022 gross county product of about US$13.1 billion (PPP) — the second-largest county economy after Nairobi — its industries include cement milling (Bamburi Cement), steel and aluminium rolling, and food and chemical processing. The former Kenya Petroleum Refineries plant ceased refining in 2013 and now operates as a fuel-import storage terminal. The city is home to the most important seaport in East Africa, Kilindini Harbour, which also serves neighbouring countries, including Uganda and parts of northern Tanzania, for their imports and exports. Kilindini is an old Swahili term meaning "deep"; the port is so called because its channel is naturally very deep. Kilindini Harbour is an example of a natural geographic phenomenon called a ria, formed at the end of the last glacial period when rising sea levels engulfed a river flowing from the mainland. Mombasa is a centre of coastal tourism in Kenya. On Mombasa Island itself the main attractions are the Old Town and Fort Jesus; the major beach resorts lie to the north (Nyali, Bamburi, Shanzu) and south (Shelly, Tiwi, Diani). The north-coast strip is known for its hotels, restaurants and nightlife.

Education Additional schools KenCada Academy; This is a school on Mombasa's mainland area of Bamburi, and practices a mixed curriculum which consists of the Kenyan curriculum, CBC and the Canadian curriculum. If counted KenCada brings the list of total International schools in Mombasa to 13. HOFACE INTERNATIONAL AUTISM SCHOOL NYALI; This is an international school located on Mombasa's mainland coast of Nyali, and specializes in teaching autistic children. Lifegate School; This is an International located on Mombasa's mainland coast of Nyali, and specializes in practicing the Accelerated Christian Education Curriculum (ACE).

Transport Air Moi International Airport is the second-largest airport in Kenya, with daily flights to Nairobi and other Kenyan, European and Middle Eastern destinations. The airport also handles substantial air cargo through its freight terminal. Rail Mombasa has a modern railway station on the Mombasa–Nairobi Standard Gauge Railway, whose Madaraka Express passenger and freight services replaced the narrow-gauge Uganda Railway completed in 1901 under British colonial rule. Completed in 2017 and located at Miritini, Mombasa Terminus links Mombasa to Nairobi; the station, about 20 kilometres from the city centre, is served by the first phase of the Dongo Kundu bypass (opened 2018). Kenya Railways transports passengers and cargo between the two cities on the SGR. Road Most roads in Mombasa are tarmacked.

Transport Sea The port of Mombasa is the largest in East Africa, with 19 deep water berths with two additional berths nearing completion and two oil terminals. The port is connected by rail and road to the interior. At present there is little or no scheduled passenger service from the port, however, international cruise ships frequent the port. The port is part of the 21st Century Maritime Silk Road that runs from the Chinese coast to the Upper Adriatic region. In connection with the Silk Road Initiative, China has started infrastructure development projects in Kenya and is building roads, railways and public buildings on credit. Ferry There is no bridge between Mombasa Island and the south coast, instead the route is served by ferries operated by the Kenya Ferry Service from Kilindini and Mtongwe to Likoni in the south coast of Mombasa. The last major accident occurred in 1994 when a ferry serving Mtongwe route sank killing more than 270 people.
